Ancistrus cryptophthalmus Reis, 1987. Common name: Bristlenose Catfish. Size: 60 mm (2.4") SL.

Type locality: Caverna Passa Três, about 300 meters into the cave, Rio São Vicente system, São Domingos, Goiás State, Brazil.

IUCN Red List: Endangered (last assessed 2018).
South America: São Vicente and Angélica-Bezerra cave system in upper Paraná River, Tocantins River drainage in Brazil.

Ancistrus should be fed mainly on vegetarian foods. Prepared foods include algae wafers and spirulina based sinking food. Vegetables such as courgette/zucchini and (English) cucumber are an excellent addition to the diet, along with the odd, small amount of more meaty foods.

A good complement to most aquariums, they are not aggressive to other species. Males may fight over territory if kept in too small a tank. Appropriate with most community fish that aren't overly big or aggressive.

Typical for the genus, with males possessing the so-called 'bushy nose'. Females may also have much smaller growths on the head, but to a much lesser extent.

Mature males and sometimes females have soft tentacles (bushy fleshy growths) on the snout - this is unique to the genus Ancistrus.

Has been bred. Tank of 100 litre, 17-25°C depending on season, with negligible daily variation, decorated with limestone. Tank was in darkness except for maintenance activities. Breeding and fry care is as for other Ancistrus species.

A blind species; living all its life in the darkness of the cave, it has lost the need for eyes and does not have any. It still has a slight medium sized spotted pattern around the head.

Etymology: Ancistrus is derived from the Greek agkistron, meaning hook, referring to the hooked interopercular odontodes. The specific epithet means hidden eyes (kryptos = hidden, ophthalmus = eyes) and refers to the cave species' lack of eyes.
Revue française d'Aquariologie Herpétologie v. 14 (no. 3), pp 82, Figs. 1, 3-4.
